17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "The linear transformation $T$ and the vector $b\in {R}^{4}$ are given below. Determine if there exists a vector $x\in {R}^{4}$ such that $T(x)=b.$
In the affirmative case, find the value of ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{4},$ where ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3},{x}_{4}$ are the components of $x.$  

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-2{x}_{4} \\ 3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}+4{x}_{4} \\ 7{x}_{4}-4{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 5 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 3 & 5 & -2 & 4 \\ -4 & -1 & -3 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Since $T$ is the standard matix of $T,$ we have $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Col}(T).$ In order to determine whether $b$ lies in $\text{Im}(T),$ we need to check if the equation $Tx=b$ is consistent. 

So, let's find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[T\,|\,b]$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & -2 & 5 \\ 3 & 5 & -2 & 4 & 5 \\ -4 & -1 & -3 & 7 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & -2 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 & -2 & 10 & -10 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 & -1 & 17 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-\frac{3}{2}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & -2 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 & -2 & 10 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -16 & 32 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has three pivot columns (the $1$st, $2$nd and the $4$th). Hence ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. 
Now, from the third equation we get 

$$
-16{x}_{4}=32\,⟹\,{x}_{4}=-2.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation gives

$$
2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}+10(-2)=-10\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=5+{x}_{3}.
$$

Then, substituting ${x}_{2}=5+{x}_{3}$ and ${x}_{4}=2$ into the first equation we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}+(5+{x}_{3})-2(-2)=5\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-4-{x}_{3}.
$$

As a result, the general solution is given by 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-4-{x}_{3} \\ 5+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{3}=0$, we have

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 5 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]
$$

where $T(x)=b.$

Finally, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{4}=-4+5-2=-1.$"} {:db/id 17592186421457 :question/id #uuid "a744da17-c832-5e19-8de7-48116074536b" :question/math-academy-id "q-38618" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124519 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9a08e0a4-22c3-5139-848d-6f1027a61056" :knowledge-point/title "Determining Whether a Vector Is in the Image of a Linear Transformation"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0ff34fdc-0a64-5ac7-9e6c-4593625c616c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{5}{8}" :db/id 17592186421431} {:answer/id #uuid "44c429a9-15eb-57f2-b546-ca949bfb2581" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{5}{3}" :db/id 17592186421436} {:answer/id #uuid "c861a1e5-85f4-5f47-a6c6-f3a0e912537f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186421443} {:answer/id #uuid "f25a09b3-86fe-5afc-8268-40b897c03f27" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "b\notin \text{Im}(T)" :db/id 17592186421449} {:answer/id #uuid "f96f6aac-f80f-53db-9b40-142a8715dce9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-12" :db/id 17592186421450}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "f25a09b3-86fe-5afc-8268-40b897c03f27" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "b\notin \text{Im}(T)" :db/id 17592186421449} :answer-field/id #uuid "971b0f6e-9510-5d58-be38-48d9da4c7303" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186421453}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "The linear transformation $T$ and the vector $b\in {R}^{4}$ are given below. In the affirmative case, find the value of $w+x-z,$ where $w,x,y,z$ are the components of $x.$  

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}w \\ x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}w+3z-x-2y \\ 4x-2w+y-6z \\ 3w+5x+10z-16y \\ 5y-w-3z-x\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -5 \\ 4 \\ 5\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 & 3 \\ -2 & 4 & 1 & -6 \\ 3 & 5 & -16 & 10 \\ -1 & -1 & 5 & -3\end{aligned}]
$$

Since $T$ is the standard matix of $T,$ we have $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Col}(T).$ In order to determine whether $b$ lies in $\text{Im}(T),$ we need to check if the equation $Tx=b$ is consistent. 

So, let's find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[T\,|\,b]$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 & 3 & 4 \\ -2 & 4 & 1 & -6 & -5 \\ 3 & 5 & -16 & 10 & 4 \\ -1 & -1 & 5 & -3 & 5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 8 & -10 & 1 & -8 \\ 0 & -2 & 3 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-4{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 1 & -20 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 12\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the fourth equation, we get the false statement $0=12.$ Therefore, the system is inconsistent, and we conclude that  $b\notin \text{Im}(T).$"} {:db/id 17592186421458 :question/id #uuid "dca0d5db-2f8d-5d5d-b6ae-e11ba42097a0" :question/math-academy-id "q-40209" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7a866058-e522-5f43-b8d1-94192b2da129" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186421438} {:answer/id #uuid "905669cb-68f2-5e43-b764-abb5dd468fd7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186421439} {:answer/id #uuid "a39cfe50-b3ce-51ec-ab4c-7ce8f1bdf7fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186421440} {:answer/id #uuid "a99db038-81b3-5562-9818-94b26695169a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "b\notin \text{Im}(T)" :db/id 17592186421441} {:answer/id #uuid "adc76ae1-1330-5825-8435-4ad0e38e48d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186421442}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186421439} :answer-field/id #uuid "1e5a8161-1b5e-5e2b-bdbc-8100f0ce6ace" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186421451}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "The standard matrix $T$ of a linear transformation $T$ and the vector $b\in {R}^{3}$ are given below. $$" :question/worked-solution "Since $T$ is the standard matix of $T,$ we have $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Col}(T).$ In order to determine whether $b$ lies in $\text{Im}(T),$ we need to check if the equation $Tx=b$ is consistent.

$$

$$

$$

$$
{x}_{1}+3({x}_{3})-2{x}_{3}=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2-{x}_{3}.

$$
[\begin{aligned}2-{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

$$

$$

where $T(x)=b.$

$\mathbf{T}$ is equivalent to the column space of its standard matrix $T.$ That is,
![](images/6e/6e8b0992ade86b8e8a0c7d2227ff5473f5cae843f8e763e556c17654e7f1f143.svg)

So to find out if a vector $\mathbf{b}$ is in the image of the linear transformation $\mathbf{T},$ we just need to check if the matrix equation $T\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is consistent." :tutorial/id #uuid "f52415b1-727f-53a7-8502-857fdcb3b835" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4276 :tutorial/title "Determining If a Vector Lies in the Image"} :step/id #uuid "cb766bed-08ee-564c-a45c-c20f57e59be3" :step/math-academy-id 25971 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125402}} {:db/id 17592186125497 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125821 :tutorial/content "In general, the rank of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ is equal to the dimension of its image:

$$
\text{rank}(\mathbf{T}) = \text{dim}(\text{Im}(\mathbf{T}))
$$

If the linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ has the standard matrix $T,$ then the dimension of the image is equal to the rank of $T{:}$

$$
\text{dim}(\text{Im}(\mathbf{T})) = \text{rank}(T)
$$

So, in general, we have

$$
\text{rank}(\mathbf{T}) = \text{rank}(T).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "89b10851-3eed-5f36-a0ab-c9d0610e9b75" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4382 :tutorial/title "The Rank of a Linear Transformation"} :step/id #uuid "9f45ab6b-4ad9-5e42-8a3f-69ef72e1a03c" :step/math-academy-id 26848 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125403}}] :activity/title "The Image and Rank of a Linear Transformation" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124748} {:db/id 17592186125401 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125783 :tutorial/content "The **image** (or **range**) of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ is the set of all vectors $\mathbf{b}$ that the transformation maps to. Determine if there exists a vector $x\in {R}^{4}$ such that $T(x)=b.$
In the affirmative case, find the value of ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{4},$ where ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3},{x}_{4}$ are the components of $x.$  

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-2{x}_{4} \\ 3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}+4{x}_{4} \\ 7{x}_{4}-4{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 5 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 3 & 5 & -2 & 4 \\ -4 & -1 & -3 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Since $T$ is the standard matix of $T,$ we have $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Col}(T).$ In order to determine whether $b$ lies in $\text{Im}(T),$ we need to check if the equation $Tx=b$ is consistent. 

So, let's find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[T\,|\,b]$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & -2 & 5 \\ 3 & 5 & -2 & 4 & 5 \\ -4 & -1 & -3 & 7 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & -2 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 & -2 & 10 & -10 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 & -1 & 17 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-\frac{3}{2}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & -2 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 & -2 & 10 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -16 & 32 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has three pivot columns (the $1$st, $2$nd and the $4$th). Hence ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. 
Now, from the third equation we get 

$$
-16{x}_{4}=32\,⟹\,{x}_{4}=-2.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation gives

$$
2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}+10(-2)=-10\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=5+{x}_{3}.
$$

Then, substituting ${x}_{2}=5+{x}_{3}$ and ${x}_{4}=2$ into the first equation we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}+(5+{x}_{3})-2(-2)=5\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-4-{x}_{3}.
$$

As a result, the general solution is given by 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-4-{x}_{3} \\ 5+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{3}=0$, we have

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 5 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]
$$

where $T(x)=b.$

Finally, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{4}=-4+5-2=-1.$"} :step/id #uuid "534ab39a-0dca-5848-9ca5-2f3c78f6a6dc" :step/next {:db/id 17592186421463}} {:db/id 17592186421461 :step/content {:db/id 17592186421456 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "19da1574-848a-5c7f-9e7b-e49c3c9a9f38" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186421433} {:answer/id #uuid "4aa7f060-fcee-5fa2-8f1c-4ce1c5c33ca7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186421437} {:answer/id #uuid "d91c8654-f35d-5e23-b5e1-a15324307faf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186421446} {:answer/id #uuid "e1f7cc0d-2061-580a-901f-09b363e7aa41" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186421447} {:answer/id #uuid "e6a9fcc8-7e10-506b-b0e1-2d66eccadcfe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186421448}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186421433} :answer-field/id #uuid "95199669-91cf-517b-ba05-3636cb7e6add" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186421452}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a248fe65-f8da-5537-9754-7384902accff" :question/math-academy-id "q-81238" :question/problem "If $T=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 5 & -3 \\ 4 & -2 & -10 & 6 \\ 2 & -1 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ is the standard matrix of the linear transformation $T$, then $\text{rank}(T)=$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $\text{rank}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Im}(T))=\text{rank}(T).$

$$" :question/worked-solution "Since $T$ is the standard matix of $T,$ we have $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Col}(T).$ In order to determine whether $b$ lies in $\text{Im}(T),$ we need to check if the equation $Tx=b$ is consistent. 

So, we find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[T\,|\,b],$ as follows:

So, let's find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[T\,|\,b]$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & -2 & 5 \\ 3 & 5 & -2 & 4 & 5 \\ -4 & -1 & -3 & 7 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & -2 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 & -2 & 10 & -10 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 & -1 & 17 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-\frac{3}{2}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & -2 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 & -2 & 10 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -16 & 32 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

:tutorial/content "Let's take a number, say, $-3.$ We can depict it on a number line as follows:

![](images/de/ded8743284f207bff35eba24617fd4245a69d439ed151d09eed564813f9d72fb.png)

The *distance* between the number $-3$ and $0$ is known as the **absolute value** of $-3.$ We write it as

$$
|-3| = {\color{red}3}.
$$

Similarly, $|\,2\,|$, the absolute value of the number $2$, is the distance between $2$ and $0$:

![](images/f4/f44fcd05fb0932083d48c8b11892247d8de8fbc46ccf7186fb12843702181aea.png)

We write $|\,2\,| = {\color{red}2}.$

So, the absolute value simply 

- *removes the minus sign*, if the number is negative, or

- does nothing, if the number is non-negative.

Sometimes, we can be asked to evaluate an expression involving the absolute value function, like $|x +1| + 5$ when $x=-3.$ In this case, we evaluate the expression inside the absolute value before simplifying the rest of the expression: 

$$
\begin{aligned}|x+1|+5 & = \\ |(-3)+1|+5 & = \\ |-2|+5 & = \\ 2+5 & = \\ 7 & \end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3325f9a7-d389-562e-ac1b-4eb26671f84b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8817 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "2ecbe2d3-3bf6-5c94-9e47-13b35a557d38" :step/math-academy-id 147765 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055549}} {:db/id 17592186055549 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054626 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054470 :question/id #uuid "af2c36f6-7258-56b3-aabc-c0736bdfb6a5" :question/math-academy-id "e-14209"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2a5017c8-1933-515c-980a-c4b6a8a46334" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048599} {:db/id 17592186049688} {:db/id 17592186050127}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055102} {:db/id 17592186055113} {:db/id 17592186055175} {:db/id 17592186481347} {:db/id 17592186481392} {:db/id 17592186481436}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating an Expression With One Absolute Value"} :step/id #uuid "4957b9ec-7c2c-553a-b341-f367fd1d5e59" :step/math-academy-id 147766 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055550}} {:db/id 17592186055550 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054627 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054471 :question/id #uuid "2af15364-dc4d-52c1-a519-02e8568279ae" :question/math-academy-id "e-14212"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9d29b448-4fd6-51bc-b2f0-92e3d909f299" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055103} {:db/id 17592186055104} {:db/id 17592186055114} {:db/id 17592186481358} {:db/id 17592186481394} {:db/id 17592186481409}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating an Expression With Two Absolute Values"} :step/id #uuid "ea43903e-13f4-5326-a1ae-670194c48ad9" :step/math-academy-id 147770}] :activity/title "Absolute Value Expressions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186054936} {:db/id 17592186055548 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056066 :tutorial/content "Let's take a number, say, $-3.$ We can depict it on a number line as follows:

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=0,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$ So, the third column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$ Computing $A-3I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{6}.$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm, we obtain the third column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{6}}{6} \\ \frac{\sqrt{6}}{3} \\ \frac{\sqrt{6}}{6}\end{aligned}]

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=0,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$ So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=0.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=0.$ Computing $A-0I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{6}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm, we obtain the first column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{6}}{6} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{6}}{3} \\ \frac{\sqrt{6}}{6}\end{aligned}]
$$"} {:db/id 17592186394963 :question/id #uuid "5bac7e35-18fd-5d08-a4e1-72c5d7aa78ae" :question/math-academy-id "q-94266"} {:db/id 17592186161989 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161781 :question/id #uuid "f6714653-0cfa-5049-9ae9-f921d46d03bb" :question/math-academy-id "e-8173"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4b16e6cc-b1ee-5ccc-91a7-980bf5fe50a5" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050578}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162600 :question/id #uuid "bba46d80-79cd-52e2-b337-86fa5c144249" :question/math-academy-id "q-93728"} {:db/id 17592186162625 :question/id #uuid "1d443cf2-e450-59f7-912e-8007eb24ac35" :question/math-academy-id "q-94332"} {:db/id 17592186357724 :question/id #uuid "10fb8494-4b1d-5103-988d-8efc21b1e895" :question/math-academy-id "q-94312"} {:db/id 17592186357732 :question/id #uuid "7fecab0a-cd00-5e03-af2a-81daa57c4cbd" :question/math-academy-id "q-94351"} {:db/id 17592186363196 :question/id #uuid "bf5de7bd-3234-5d41-a9a5-c12fb9a085ef" :question/math-academy-id "q-140841"} {:db/id 17592186364530 :question/id #uuid "bc0d6469-4523-5a6a-b241-3d642027e56c" :question/math-academy-id "q-94345"} {:db/id 17592186404693 :question/id #uuid "f0919d70-c1a2-5d35-a661-b7830e88967b" :question/math-academy-id "q-94347"} {:db/id 17592186404700 :question/id #uuid "8750edd7-2f06-5edf-8b79-4b30e6b68324" :question/math-academy-id "q-94372"}] :knowledge-point/title "Orthogonally Diagonalizing a 3x3 Matrix With Repeated Eigenvalues"} {:db/id 17592186161781 :question/id #uuid "f6714653-0cfa-5049-9ae9-f921d46d03bb" :question/math-academy-id "e-8173" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186161989 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4b16e6cc-b1ee-5ccc-91a7-980bf5fe50a5" :knowledge-point/title "Orthogonally Diagonalizing a 3x3 Matrix With Repeated Eigenvalues"}] :question/problem "![](images/5c/5cad03639230a7935a92ab107ec04502b0c8caa42c8fd72589b151d8da8fcd2e.png)

$$
A=PDP^T,
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D=P^TAP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D=P^T \! AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are $\lambda_1=-1,$ $\lambda_2=-1,$ and $\lambda_3=8.$ So, the first and second columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-1.$ 

Now, we need to find eigenvectors that correspond to $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives two eigenvectors: 

$\qquad$ ![](images/0f/0f63b25d6d3527f5862ce68bea82cc1624630795d98226e144400da6bdc90ee4.png) and ![](images/5b/5be366991cc864298313b9b38f0a1cd252d7dbe8a237ab5d3cfe5e5e2f98eecf.png)

Notice that eigenvectors $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set 
![](images/7c/7c24fd26d331372c96a26011c366aa8e3d51e88c2ac654d07c0d5fd377c672c2.png)
and we find $\mathbf{e}_2$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}_{2} & ={v}_{2}-\frac{{v}_{2}\cdot {e}_{1}}{{e}_{1}\cdot {e}_{1}}{e}_{1} \\  & ={v}_{2}-\frac{1}{5}{e}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{4}{5} \\ -\frac{2}{5} \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=4,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=9.$ So, the first and second columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2}.$ 

Now, we need to find eigenvectors that correspond to ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Computing $A-4I,$ we get  

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 8\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives two eigenvectors: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$

Notice that eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are orthogonal. Finally, dividing ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖} & =\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ \frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$ So, the second and third columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}={\lambda }_{3}=3.$ Computing $A-3I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives two eigenvectors: 

$\,$ ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$

Notice that eigenvectors ${v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set 

$$
{e}_{2}={v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}],
$$

and we find ${e}_{3}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}_{3} & ={v}_{3}-\frac{{v}_{3}\cdot {e}_{2}}{{e}_{2}\cdot {e}_{2}}{e}_{2} \\  & ={v}_{3}-\frac{1}{5}{e}_{2} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ 2 \\ -\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, dividing ${e}_{2}$ and ${e}_{3}$ by their respective norms, we obtain the second and third columns of $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}_{2}}{‖{e}_{2}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ 0 \\ \frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{aligned}] \\ \frac{{e}_{3}}{‖{e}_{3}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{24}{5}}}[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ 2 \\ -\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{30}}{15} \\ \frac{\sqrt{30}}{6} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{30}}{30}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186363196 :question/id #uuid "bf5de7bd-3234-5d41-a9a5-c12fb9a085ef" :question/math-academy-id "q-140841"} {:db/id 17592186364530 :question/id #uuid "bc0d6469-4523-5a6a-b241-3d642027e56c" :question/math-academy-id "q-94345" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186161989 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4b16e6cc-b1ee-5ccc-91a7-980bf5fe50a5" :knowledge-point/title "Orthogonally Diagonalizing a 3x3 Matrix With Repeated Eigenvalues"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "33d33072-0e95-532d-bfe9-f8a1d3590433" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}]$

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=8.$ So, the first and second columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-1.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives two eigenvectors: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$

Notice that eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set 

$$
{e}_{1}={v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

and we find ${e}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}_{2} & ={v}_{2}-\frac{{v}_{2}\cdot {e}_{1}}{{e}_{1}\cdot {e}_{1}}{e}_{1} \\  & ={v}_{2}-\frac{1}{2}{e}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, dividing ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}_{1}}{‖{e}_{1}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}] \\ \frac{{e}_{2}}{‖{e}_{2}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{9}{2}}}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6} \\ \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186404693 :question/id #uuid "f0919d70-c1a2-5d35-a661-b7830e88967b" :question/math-academy-id "q-94347"} {:db/id 17592186404700 :question/id #uuid "8750edd7-2f06-5edf-8b79-4b30e6b68324" :question/math-academy-id "q-94372"} {:db/id 17592186161990 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161782 :question/id #uuid "4779b6be-97c9-5389-b25e-e8f438f0a7fd" :question/math-academy-id "e-8175"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "77a2b06b-e239-59a5-8af0-6cbbf27c3c08" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048493}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162598 :question/id #uuid "c2f119be-4dbb-5583-8e23-114609166369" :question/math-academy-id "q-93726"} {:db/id 17592186162623 :question/id #uuid "64cf1141-3501-5dd0-bfea-c963489f6fe0" :question/math-academy-id "q-94254"} {:db/id 17592186357704 :question/id #uuid "1450475b-c2c3-5f2d-978f-08f4b4041ef9" :question/math-academy-id "q-94250"} {:db/id 17592186357705 :question/id #uuid "c497ac69-8d8c-5ea0-b36e-659d4cac4441" :question/math-academy-id "q-94253"} {:db/id 17592186357706 :question/id #uuid "aa2a5fda-40ff-59dc-b588-ee085fb956e9" :question/math-academy-id "q-94256"} {:db/id 17592186364523 :question/id #uuid "3f089fe0-4b54-5b70-8e16-3f5b0bfd567e" :question/math-academy-id "q-94251"}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Parts of an Orthogonal Diagonalization"} {:db/id 17592186161782 :question/id #uuid "4779b6be-97c9-5389-b25e-e8f438f0a7fd" :question/math-academy-id "e-8175" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186161990 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "77a2b06b-e239-59a5-8af0-6cbbf27c3c08" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Parts of an Orthogonal Diagonalization"}] :question/problem "![](images/cc/cc6da0a8cce346291ba1fd50fa1fe7fad0f79558e405dc521f9a7886ec035b41.png)

$[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$" :db/id 17592186356905} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186162848} :activity/id #uuid "a251e410-6f92-5d37-91f6-3fe7f0377f20" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050539 :topic/id #uuid "52089b25-b5c5-5717-906a-bd765cce0502" :topic/math-academy-id 3119} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186162848 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163223 :tutorial/content "Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PDP^T,
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a real matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

The procedure for finding an orthogonal diagonalization of a $3 \times 3$ symmetric matrix $A$ is similar to diagonalizing a regular (diagonalizable) $3\times 3$ matrix:

- **Step 1**: Find the eigenvalues of $A.$

- **Step 2**: Find a basis of  $\mathbb{R}^3$ consisting of *unit orthogonal* eigenvectors of $A.$

- **Step 3**: Construct the matrices $D$ and $P.$

As an example, consider the matrix 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2 & -5 & 1 \\ -5 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -8\end{aligned}]
$$

This matrix is symmetric. So let's apply our diagonalization algorithm.

- **Step 1.**  We find the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving $\det(A-\lambda I)=0.$ This gives

$$
\lambda_1=3, \qquad \lambda_2=-6, \qquad \lambda_3=-9.
$$

- **Step 2.** We need to find an eigenvector basis of $\mathbb R^3.$ Seeking a nonzero solution of $|A-\lambda_i I| = 0$ for $i=1,2,3,$ we get the corresponding eigenvectors

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that the eigenvectors are mutually orthogonal. 
Now, an orthogonal diagonalization requires each eigenvector to be normalized. So, dividing each eigenvector by its norm, we obtain the following unit orthogonal eigenvectors:

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

- **Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the orthogonal matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -9\end{aligned}]
$$

**Watch out!** In this example, we automatically get orthogonal eigenvectors because $A$ has three *distinct* eigenvalues. However, in the case of repeated eigenvalues, the corresponding eigenvectors might not be orthogonal." :tutorial/id #uuid "0ff932ad-00a4-58cd-952f-55c21e02ef43" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4881 {:db/id 17592186162915 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163249 :tutorial/content "Let's recall the algorithm for diagonalizing a $3\times 3$ symmetric matrix $A.$

- **Step 1**: Find the eigenvalues of $A.$

- **Step 2**: Find a basis of  $\mathbb{R}^3$ consisting of unit orthogonal eigenvectors of $A.$

- **Step 3**: Construct the matrices $D$ and $P.$

Note the following important points regarding step 2 of this process:

- If $A$ has mutually distinct eigenvalues, the eigenvectors will automatically be orthogonal, so we only need to normalize them.

- If $A$ has *repeated* eigenvalues, then the eigenvectors corresponding to these repeated eigenvalues *may not* be orthogonal. Therefore, we have to apply the Gram-Schmidt process to obtain orthogonal vectors.

For example, consider the following matrix:

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

This matrix is symmetric. Let's apply our diagonalization algorithm.

- **Step 1.**  We find the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving $\det(A-\lambda I)=0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\lambda_1=4, \qquad \lambda_2=4, \qquad \lambda_3=-2
$$

- **Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $\mathbb R^3.$ Seeking a nonzero solution of $|A-\lambda_i I| = 0$ for $i=1,2,3,$ we get the corresponding eigenvectors

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

and we find $\mathbf{e}_2$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}_{2} & ={v}_{2}-\frac{{v}_{2}\cdot {e}_{1}}{{e}_{1}\cdot {e}_{1}}{e}_{1} \\  & ={v}_{2}-\frac{1}{2}{e}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-(-\frac{1}{2})[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, the vectors $\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2$ and $\mathbf v_3$ form an *orthogonal* basis of $\mathbb R^3.$ Dividing each eigenvector by its norm, we obtain the unit orthogonal eigenvectors:

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

- **Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6ad655c9-a00e-5174-a98f-6ae8ab07843d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5013 :tutorial/title "Symmetric Matrices With Repeated Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "63db5c7a-ccd4-5948-af8b-421d4a60d2da" :step/math-academy-id 31356 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162871}}] :activity/title "Diagonalization of 3x3 Symmetric Matrices" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186162215} {:db/id 17592186162848 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163223 :tutorial/content "Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

- If $A$ has *repeated* eigenvalues, then the eigenvectors corresponding to these repeated eigenvalues *may not* be orthogonal. Therefore, we have to apply the Gram-Schmidt process to obtain orthogonal vectors.

For example, consider the following matrix:

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

This matrix is symmetric. Let's apply our diagonalization algorithm.

- **Step 1.**  We find the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving $\det(A-\lambda I)=0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\lambda_1=4, \qquad \lambda_2=4, \qquad \lambda_3=-2
$$

- **Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $\mathbb R^3.$ Seeking a nonzero solution of $|A-\lambda_i I| = 0$ for $i=1,2,3,$ we get the corresponding eigenvectors

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

and we find $\mathbf{e}_2$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}_{2} & ={v}_{2}-\frac{{v}_{2}\cdot {e}_{1}}{{e}_{1}\cdot {e}_{1}}{e}_{1} \\  & ={v}_{2}-\frac{1}{2}{e}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-(-\frac{1}{2})[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, the vectors $\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2$ and $\mathbf v_3$ form an *orthogonal* basis of $\mathbb R^3.$ Dividing each eigenvector by its norm, we obtain the unit orthogonal eigenvectors:

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

- **Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6ad655c9-a00e-5174-a98f-6ae8ab07843d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5013 :tutorial/title "Symmetric Matrices With Repeated Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "63db5c7a-ccd4-5948-af8b-421d4a60d2da" :step/math-academy-id 31356 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162871}} {:db/id 17592186162871 :step/content {:db/id 17592186161989 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161781 :question/id #uuid "f6714653-0cfa-5049-9ae9-f921d46d03bb" :question/math-academy-id "e-8173"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4b16e6cc-b1ee-5ccc-91a7-980bf5fe50a5" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050578}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162600} {:db/id 17592186162625} {:db/id 17592186357724} {:db/id 17592186357732} {:db/id 17592186363196} {:db/id 17592186364530} {:db/id 17592186404693} {:db/id 17592186404700}] :knowledge-point/title "Orthogonally Diagonalizing a 3x3 Matrix With Repeated Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "e9df74bd-9e6b-5113-a23f-86c30ccc850b" :step/math-academy-id 30595} {:db/id 17592186163249 :tutorial/content "Let's recall the algorithm for diagonalizing a $3\times 3$ symmetric matrix $A.$

$$

and we find $\mathbf{e}_2$ as follows:

\begin{aligned}{e}_{2} & ={v}_{2}-\frac{{v}_{2}\cdot {e}_{1}}{{e}_{1}\cdot {e}_{1}}{e}_{1} \\  & ={v}_{2}-\frac{1}{2}{e}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-(-\frac{1}{2})[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

Notice that in diagrams I, II and III we have bisectors but they are not perpendicular to $\overline{AB}$."} {:db/id 17592186048723} {:db/id 17592186074187 :question/id #uuid "73201912-9dec-549a-8fa2-c88228795eab" :question/math-academy-id "q-52809"} {:db/id 17592186074193 :question/id #uuid "47a77387-c99f-5b99-a7d9-6ecb967c9323" :question/math-academy-id "q-53025"} {:db/id 17592186073877 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073585 :question/id #uuid "01b53ce1-80d9-530a-bfba-cfd500b37f9d" :question/math-academy-id "e-2610"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5cda2e87-1a65-5075-96fd-98a8a4fd7d7a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186074189 :question/id #uuid "e7525286-69d7-50c5-a30b-c8f52117c666" :question/math-academy-id "q-52978"} {:db/id 17592186074190 :question/id #uuid "60defaf0-167b-5cd2-81fb-25f259c59fe2" :question/math-academy-id "q-52979"} {:db/id 17592186233250 :question/id #uuid "5eb073ff-ce4e-55ca-b494-a85439f15398" :question/math-academy-id "q-118638"}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Perpendicular Bisector Theorem"} {:db/id 17592186073585 :question/id #uuid "01b53ce1-80d9-530a-bfba-cfd500b37f9d" :question/math-academy-id "e-2610" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186073877 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5cda2e87-1a65-5075-96fd-98a8a4fd7d7a" :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Perpendicular Bisector Theorem"}] :question/problem "Solve for $x$ in the figure below given that $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{CD}$ is the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AB}$.

![](images/2d/2dea948c7ab1cf3bb7f543c651d98f23cda8531bbec8cc44e12736c3f04f04c3.png)" :question/worked-solution "By the perpendicular bisector theorem, a point on the perpendicular bisector of a segment is equidistant from the endpoints of the segment. Hence, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}
DA &= DB \\

\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186074189 :question/id #uuid "e7525286-69d7-50c5-a30b-c8f52117c666" :question/math-academy-id "q-52978"} {:db/id 17592186074190 :question/id #uuid "60defaf0-167b-5cd2-81fb-25f259c59fe2" :question/math-academy-id "q-52979"} {:db/id 17592186233250 :question/id #uuid "5eb073ff-ce4e-55ca-b494-a85439f15398" :question/math-academy-id "q-118638"} {:db/id 17592186073878 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073586 :question/id #uuid "ab4fe8cf-3651-5a1f-a796-546892cb0178" :question/math-academy-id "e-2613"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "25e57b78-5159-51bc-aeaf-9530f641262b" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186074191 :question/id #uuid "d6ad8f39-1f2a-5577-a0c9-c232f1e96abf" :question/math-academy-id "q-52983"} {:db/id 17592186074192 :question/id #uuid "01196150-b312-53cd-948a-5e1de72a8c55" :question/math-academy-id "q-53024"}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Converse of the Perpendicular Bisector Theorem"} {:db/id 17592186073586 :question/id #uuid "ab4fe8cf-3651-5a1f-a796-546892cb0178" :question/math-academy-id "e-2613" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186073878 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "25e57b78-5159-51bc-aeaf-9530f641262b" :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Converse of the Perpendicular Bisector Theorem"}] :question/problem "Solve for $x$ in the figure below given that $AD=BD$ and $AE=BE$.

![](images/e5/e58ea5aadf9075a8b1d7a3de3a3c82e88eb3b47281cf75134631d3a153d42127.png)" :question/worked-solution "By the converse of the perpendicular bisector theorem, a point equidistant from the endpoints of a segment lies on the perpendicular bisector of the segment.

Here, the points $D$ and $E$ are both equidistant from the endpoints of $\overline{AB}$. Therefore, $D$ and $E$ both lie on the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AB}$.

Since only one line can be drawn through two given points, the line $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{DE}$ is the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AB}$.

In particular, we have that $AC=BC$. We can use this equation to solve for $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
AC &= BC \\
3x + 2 &= 5x - 2 \\
4 &= 2x \\
x &= 2
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186074191 :question/id #uuid "d6ad8f39-1f2a-5577-a0c9-c232f1e96abf" :question/math-academy-id "q-52983"} {:db/id 17592186074192 :question/id #uuid "01196150-b312-53cd-948a-5e1de72a8c55" :question/math-academy-id "q-53024"} {:db/id 17592186048216} {:db/id 17592186048360} {:db/id 17592186048472} {:db/id 17592186048718} {:db/id 17592186049564} {:db/id 17592186050103} {:db/id 17592186050160} {:db/id 17592186050365} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186074863} :activity/id #uuid "37e46b78-af93-563c-9c22-49fec2ac17ef" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050357 :topic/id #uuid "4226fd5b-b1b5-57e0-a1c2-d40bfd3ac949" :topic/math-academy-id 521} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186074863 :step/content {:db/id 17592186074976 :tutorial/content "Two intersecting lines are **perpendicular** if they form a right angle (an angle that measures $90^\circ$).

![](images/ee/ee6258a8a148ae3a8f4ce63321bf9f4dfa955eb0a90b332477e6cc933cad7b74.png)

For example, the two lines above are perpendicular because the angle $\angle BOD$ is a right angle.

The opposite is also true: if two lines are perpendicular, then they meet at a right angle.

As you may have noticed already, when two lines are perpendicular, they don't form only one right angle. All the four angles formed by the intersection are right angles!

![](images/15/152aa56c4fd669e417cb20f1bef8fcec7e7ea34e0be9e44e7acad3ac490e5713.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "ffd3b7d9-a64e-5147-bd6d-d2892a17bbb9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2185 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "30171190-d63a-5632-937f-c723296dc4a5" :step/math-academy-id 73809 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074864}} {:db/id 17592186074864 :step/content {:db/id 17592186075003 :tutorial/content "A segment **bisector** is any segment, line, or ray that splits another segment into two congruent parts.

For example, in the diagram below, $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{AB}$ is a bisector of the segment $\overline{ST}$.

![](images/1c/1cf8d2956dd054509cb421a1b706063ea318f14d0575295634baf0fc5679105c.png)

A **perpendicular bisector** is any segment, line, or ray that bisects another segment *and is perpendicular to that segment*.

For example, in the diagram below, $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{UV}$ is a perpendicular bisector of the segment $\overline{ST}$.

![](images/01/01cf976113ad5c2f635548aab38434c4add38c61195aacc96e611077aa4df606.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "b4e7bceb-cc96-58c7-b89d-38f59696caaa" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3122 :tutorial/title "Bisectors"} :step/id #uuid "ea487a60-e3d3-53f8-8fe6-f94b5665c98a" :step/math-academy-id 73810 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074865}} {:db/id 17592186074865 :step/content {:db/id 17592186073876 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073584 :question/id #uuid "d49eb5a2-baaf-527f-bfa7-12b2befa865a" :question/math-academy-id "e-2609"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5fbb6558-01d5-5d08-8e84-64077353b2a6" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048723} {:db/id 17592186050476}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186074187} {:db/id 17592186074193}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Properties of Perpendicular Bisectors"} :step/id #uuid "a66c9782-dc26-51cf-a396-ca74eae155be" :step/math-academy-id 73811 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074866}} {:db/id 17592186074866 :step/content {:db/id 17592186074987 :tutorial/content "The **perpendicular bisector theorem** states that:

> In a plane, if a point is on the perpendicular bisector of a segment, then it is equidistant from the endpoints of the segment.

For example, in the diagram below, we see that $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{CD}$ is the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AB}$.

![](images/b4/b45782d21e6ffdff1fd46956b1933d976df90e69f8d5e15e2edf116fe11c0e8e.png)

Consequently, we can conclude that the point $D$ is equidistant from the endpoints of $\overline{AB}$. So we have $AD=BD$." :tutorial/id #uuid "eefe034d-1e7e-55b2-9f1c-58f2df60defc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2360 :tutorial/title "The Perpendicular Bisector Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "c0f78ca3-27f5-5550-9f9e-4a6e83a3019a" :step/math-academy-id 73814 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074867}} {:db/id 17592186074867 :step/content {:db/id 17592186073877 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073585 :question/id #uuid "01b53ce1-80d9-530a-bfba-cfd500b37f9d" :question/math-academy-id "e-2610"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5cda2e87-1a65-5075-96fd-98a8a4fd7d7a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186074189} {:db/id 17592186074190} {:db/id 17592186233250}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Perpendicular Bisector Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "e41c50b6-9fa3-57d8-8d33-d797739dc3d7" :step/math-academy-id 73815 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074868}} {:db/id 17592186074868 :step/content {:db/id 17592186074988 :tutorial/content "The **converse of the perpendicular bisector theorem** states that:

> In a plane, if a point is equidistant from the endpoints of a segment, then it is on the perpendicular bisector of the segment.

For example, in the diagram below, we see that $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{CD}$ is perpendicular to $\overline{AB}$, and the point $D$ is equidistant from the endpoints of $\overline{AB}$.

![](images/d1/d17f25984a6e153a6f155552e7da4a0d67241ad7e83eabefb5ad5b663827fbce.png)

Therefore, we can conclude that $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{CD}$ is the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AB}$. In particular, we conclude that $AC = BC$." :tutorial/id #uuid "2224f56e-4101-55a0-9dd0-05903bc3226b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2361 :tutorial/title "The Converse of the Perpendicular Bisector Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "3eb6ca80-41aa-5855-a721-79268fd23a3a" :step/math-academy-id 73818 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074869}} {:db/id 17592186074869 :step/content {:db/id 17592186073878 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073586 :question/id #uuid "ab4fe8cf-3651-5a1f-a796-546892cb0178" :question/math-academy-id "e-2613"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "25e57b78-5159-51bc-aeaf-9530f641262b" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186074191} {:db/id 17592186074192}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Converse of the Perpendicular Bisector Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "5f561bba-2e4e-56f5-b6aa-667b06db1509" :step/math-academy-id 73819 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074870}} {:db/id 17592186074870 :step/content {:db/id 17592186075002 :tutorial/content "The most important property of perpendicular lines is the following.

> Given a line $l$ and a point $P$, there is one and only one line $m$ that passes through $P$ and is perpendicular to $l$.

![](images/24/24e78b2f90aa4cfd9a6eba5ace46195536377c19d255e51e82485af69c866292.png)

Other nice properties include the following:

- If two distinct lines are perpendicular to the same (third) line, then these two lines are parallel. For example, in the figure below, both lines $n$ and $m$ are perpendicular to the line $l$. As a result, $n \parallel m$.
- If a line is perpendicular to one of two parallel lines, then that line is also perpendicular to the second parallel line.

![](images/64/64bae80f45df4e2536e3c929471352e9d911607efeeab9bd835acebf4ff0af01.png)

Symbol $\perp$

Finally, if a line $p$ is perpendicular to a line $q$, we can denote it without words using the symbol $\perp$ (perpendicular), as follows:

$$
p \perp q
$$

This reads as "*$p$ is perpendicular to $q$*."" :tutorial/id #uuid "b323a149-5fd9-529b-8eb0-28a8cd06e56c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2985 :tutorial/title "Basic Properties of Perpendicular Lines"} :step/id #uuid "f9beea6b-dcdf-5676-8112-d86aa617b006" :step/math-academy-id 73822}] :activity/title "Segment Bisectors and the Perpendicular Bisector Theorem" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186073943} {:db/id 17592186074863 :step/content {:db/id 17592186074976 :tutorial/content "Two intersecting lines are **perpendicular** if they form a right angle (an angle that measures $90^\circ$).

The opposite is also true: if two lines are perpendicular, then they meet at a right angle.

As you may have noticed already, when two lines are perpendicular, they don't form only one right angle. All the four angles formed by the intersection are right angles!

> Given a line $l$ and a point $P$, there is one and only one line $m$ that passes through $P$ and is perpendicular to $l$.

![](images/24/24e78b2f90aa4cfd9a6eba5ace46195536377c19d255e51e82485af69c866292.png)

Other nice properties include the following:

- If two distinct lines are perpendicular to the same (third) line, then these two lines are parallel. For example, in the figure below, both lines $n$ and $m$ are perpendicular to the line $l$. As a result, $n \parallel m$.
- If a line is perpendicular to one of two parallel lines, then that line is also perpendicular to the second parallel line.

![](images/64/64bae80f45df4e2536e3c929471352e9d911607efeeab9bd835acebf4ff0af01.png)

Symbol $\perp$

Finally, if a line $p$ is perpendicular to a line $q$, we can denote it without words using the symbol $\perp$ (perpendicular), as follows:

$$
p \perp q
$$

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "Given a linear transformation over ${R}^{2}$ with the standard matrix $T,$ we have the following:

- $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto ${R}^{2}$ if and only if $\text{rank}(T)=2,$ i.e., $T$ is nonsingular.

- $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto a line if and only if $\text{rank}(T)=1.$

- $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto $(0,0)$ if and only if $\text{rank}(T)=0,$ i.e., $T$ is the zero matrix.

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- ${T}_{1}$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto a line. Notice that the columns of ${T}_{1}$ are linearly dependent but it's not the zero matrix. So, $\text{rank}({T}_{1})=1.$

- ${T}_{2}$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto $(0,0)$ since ${T}_{2}$ is the zero matrix, i.e. $\text{rank}({T}_{2})=0.$

- ${T}_{3}$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto ${R}^{2}.$ Indeed, ${T}_{3}$ is a nonsingular matrix, i.e. $\text{rank}({T}_{3})=2.$

transformation $\mathbf{T}$ that maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto the line $y=-5x.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $\langle -1, 5 \rangle \in \text{Im}(\mathbf{T})$

- $\textrm{Ker}(\mathbf{T})=\{0\}$

- $\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{T})=\Bbb R^2$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that when the image of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the standard matrix $T$ is a one-dimensional line, then

$$
\textrm{rank}(T) = \textrm{rank}(\mathbf{T}) = 1,
$$

and, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T) & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the point $(-1,5)$ satisfies the equation of the line $y=-5x$ since $5=-5\cdot (-1).$ Hence, 

$$
\langle -1, 5 \rangle \in \textrm{Im}(\mathbf{T}).
$$

- Statement II is false. Since $\textrm{nullity}(T)=1,$ we get 

$$
\textrm{Ker}(\mathbf{T}) \neq \{\mathbf0\}.
$$

- Statement III is false.  Since $\textrm{rank}(\mathbf{T})=1,$ we get 

$$
\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{T}) \neq \Bbb R^2.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} {:db/id 17592186048978} {:db/id 17592186049340} {:db/id 17592186049903} {:db/id 17592186176273 :question/id #uuid "86bc6bae-46fe-5b21-aa49-70bad1578afa" $$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=0
$$

and, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T) & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. In our case, we have 

$$
\text{rank}(T)=0.
$$

- Statement II is false. The image of $T$ contains the vector zero vector $0=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the condition $\text{nullity}(T)=2$ in ${R}^{2}$ is equivalent to 

$$
\text{Ker}(T)={R}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only.""} {:db/id 17592186360751 :question/id #uuid "2667e6b9-8784-550d-a849-0ee298d78d90" :question/math-academy-id "q-97078"} {:db/id 17592186366052 :question/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "If the linear transformation $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto the line $5y=6x$ then, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $⟨\frac{6}{5},1⟩\in \text{Im}(T)$

- **II.** $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}$

- **III.** $\text{nullity}(T)=0$, where $T$ is the standard matrix of $T$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that when the image of a linear transformation $T$ in ${R}^{2}$ with the standard matrix $T$ is a one-dimensional line, then

$$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=1
$$

and, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T) & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn. 

- Statement I is false.
Notice that the point $(\frac{6}{5},1)$ does not satisfy the equation of the line $5y=6x$ since $5\cdot 1\ne \frac{6}{5}\cdot 6.$ Therefore, 
$⟨\frac{6}{5},1⟩\notin \text{Im}(T).$

- Statement II is true.
Since $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto a line passing through the origin, we have that the standard matrix $T$ is singular. So, $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}.$

- Statement III is false.
Since  statement II is true we have that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim(Ker}(T))\ne 0.$"} {:db/id 17592186366773 :question/id #uuid "cbb0c470-3f82-5cd2-8de9-680715504460" :question/math-academy-id Select all that apply.

- **I.** $⟨2,1⟩\in \text{Im}(T)$
- **II.** $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}$
- **III.** $\text{nullity}(T)=2$, where $T$ is the standard matrix of $T$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that when the image of a linear transformation $T$ in ${R}^{2}$ with the standard matrix $T$ is a one-dimensional line, then

$$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=1,
$$

and, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T) & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. The point $(2,1)$ does not satisfy the equation of the line $y=2x$ since $1\ne 2\cdot 2.$ Hence, 

$$
⟨2,1⟩\notin \text{Im}(T).
$$

- Statement II is true. Since $\text{nullity}(T)=1,$ we get 

$$
\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}.
$$

- Statement III is false. We have that 

$$
\text{nullity}(T)=1.
$$

[{:db/id 17592186176932 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177088 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the following linear transformation:

$$\mathbf{T}: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$$

The image of $\mathbf{T}$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Therefore, it can only be one of the following:

- the whole of $\mathbb{R}^2,$
- a line through the origin, or
- a single point (vector), namely the origin $(0,0).$

Let's denote the standard matrix of $\mathbf{T}$ by $T.$ It turns out that the dimension of the image of $\mathbf{T}$ depends on $\text{rank}(T)$ (or equivalently on $\text{nullity}(T)$ by the rank-nullity theorem). Indeed, we have the following:

- If $\textrm{rank}(T)=2,$ then the two columns of $T$ are linearly independent. This means $T$ is invertible and therefore, $\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{T}) = \mathbb{R}^2.$

For example, the following transformation maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto $\mathbb{R}^2\mathbin{:}$ $$T= [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]$$

![](images/88/88baa47cae14d4a43d59b366c13b3c29376678edef2fe34ff505a942ef6af986.png)

- If $\textrm{rank}(T)=1,$ then there is a nonzero vector that generates the image of $\mathbf{T}.$ In this case, the image of $\mathbf{T}$ is a one-dimensional subspace of $\Bbb R^2$. So, it is a line passing through the origin.

For example, the following transformation maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto the line $y=2x\mathbin{:}$ $$T= [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}]$$ Notice that the points $(2,4)$ and $(1,2),$ defined by the columns of $T,$ lie on the line $y=2x.$

![](images/03/0322f183c16fe82515277d10cf27a93ae753f8eadf7eeb1db4d3c5e404480b09.png)

- If $\textrm{rank}(T)=0$ then, according to the rank-nullity theorem, $$\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =\text{nullity}(T) \\ & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\ & =2-0 \\ & =2.\end{aligned}$$ This means that $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{0}$ for all $\mathbf{v}\in \Bbb R^2$. So, in this case, we have that $$T= [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],$$ which maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto $\{(0,0)\},$ i.e., the set containing only the zero vector $\mathbf{0}.$

- If $\textrm{rank}(T)=1,$ then there is a nonzero vector that generates the image of $\mathbf{T}.$ In this case, the image of $\mathbf{T}$ is a one-dimensional subspace of $\Bbb R^2$. So, it is a line passing through the origin.

For example, the following transformation maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto the line $y=2x\mathbin{:}$ $$T= [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}]$$ Notice that the points $(2,4)$ and $(1,2),$ defined by the columns of $T,$ lie on the line $y=2x.$

![](images/03/0322f183c16fe82515277d10cf27a93ae753f8eadf7eeb1db4d3c5e404480b09.png)

- If $\textrm{rank}(T)=0$ then, according to the rank-nullity theorem, $$\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =\text{nullity}(T) \\ & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\ & =2-0 \\ & =2.\end{aligned}$$ This means that $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{0}$ for all $\mathbf{v}\in \Bbb R^2$. So, in this case, we have that $$T= [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],$$ which maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto $\{(0,0)\},$ i.e., the set containing only the zero vector $\mathbf{0}.$

- $B_1, B_2,$ and $B_3$ are *mutually exclusive*, and

- the events $B_1, B_2,$ and $B_3$ cover the *entire* sample space.

When these two conditions are satisfied, we say that $\mathcal S$ is the **disjoint union** of  $B_1, B_2,$ and $B_3,$ and we write 
 

$$
\mathcal S = B_1 \sqcup B_2 \sqcup B_3.
$$

A diagram of this situation is shown below. Notice that $B_1, B_2,$ and $B_3$ cover the entire diagram but do not overlap.

![](images/f5/f5f9f04eb6affb9dca1f7d4e7d66d76c4d520cbf66db93db60639ce896fb19af.png)

 

Now suppose that we wish to compute the probability of an event $A$ that lies within $\mathcal S.$ Let's draw this event on our diagram and label its intersections with $B_1, B_2, B_3\mathbin{:}$

![](images/ed/ed6568369a3af39cf1f6ecd5cb481de20d6c31bbce0fa1be54eb9ae0ab4e7f20.png)

 

The **law of total probability** can be deduced from this diagram. It states that

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =P(A\cap {B}_{1})+P(A\cap {B}_{2})+P(A\cap {B}_{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

In this lesson, we will only consider a disjoint union of $\mathcal S$ consisting of three events. However, it should be noted that the law of total probability can be extended to an arbitrary number of events, that is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =P(A\cap {B}_{1})+P(A\cap {B}_{2})+⋯ \\  & ={\sum }_{i}P(A\cap {B}_{i})\end{aligned}
$$

where $\mathcal S = B_1 \sqcup B_2\sqcup \ldots$ is a disjoint union of $\mathcal S.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d4103a1f-00a1-55d2-8e99-f1b230f8b348" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6295 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "34e9e254-fd36-5512-88cc-6abf808e561b" :step/math-academy-id 836329 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093206}} {:db/id 17592186093202 :step/content {:db/id 17592186092314 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186091925 :question/id #uuid "c690991e-6029-5067-b97a-67c5e62b7f47" :question/math-academy-id "e-10109"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4149b2fe-4243-595e-af7f-851b308f7eb1" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050990}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186092557} {:db/id 17592186092562} {:db/id 17592186436222} {:db/id 17592186436226} {:db/id 17592186436229} {:db/id 17592186436234}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Law of Total Probability"} :step/id #uuid "92a781b8-11f6-5279-b328-89be09bb0155" :step/math-academy-id 836331 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093203}} {:db/id 17592186093203 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093476 :tutorial/content "The law of total probability states that

$$

There are $10$ roses in the first plot, of which $5$ are red, $12$ roses in the second plot, of which $6$ are red, and $14$ roses in the third plot, of which $4$ are red. What is the probability that a randomly selected rose from the garden is red?

Let $A$ be the event that a chosen rose is red, and 

- let $B_1$ be the event that the selected rose comes from the first plot,

- let $B_2$ be the event that the selected rose comes from the second plot,

- let $B_3$ be the event that the selected rose comes from the third plot.

Notice that the disjoint union

$$
B_1\sqcup B_2\sqcup B_3
$$

covers the entire sample space, and that there are a total of 

$$
10+12+14=36
$$

roses in the garden. 

- To calculate $P(A \cap B_1),$ we take the number of red roses in the first plot $(5)$ and divide by the total number of roses $(36).$ So, we have 

$$
P(A \cap B_1) = \dfrac{5}{36}.
$$

- To calculate $P(A \cap B_2),$ we take the number of red roses in the second plot $(6)$ and divide by the total number of roses $(36).$ So, we have 

$$
P(A \cap B_2) = \dfrac{6}{36}.
$$

- To calculate $P(A \cap B_3),$ we take the number of red roses in the third plot $(4)$ and divide by the total number of roses $(36).$ So, we have 

$$
P(A \cap B_3) = \dfrac{4}{36}.
$$

So, to calculate the probability that a randomly chosen rose is red, we use the law of total probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =P(A\cap {B}_{1})+P(A\cap {B}_{2})+P(A\cap {B}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{5}{36}+\frac{6}{36}+\frac{4}{36} \\  & =\frac{15}{36} \\  & =\frac{5}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

   

Note the following: 

- You may have noticed that there is an easier way to solve this problem. That is, to sum the total number of red roses $(5+6+4 = 15)$ and divide by the total number of roses $(10+12+14 = 36).$ However, you're encouraged to work with the law of total probability as it's essential to get used to the concept.

- A little later in this lesson, we'll work with a version of the law of total probability that isn't intuitive. Understanding the law of total probability in its simplest form will help when things get trickier.

![](images/6d/6d39f6b553856204eb1958c84fb06dc2756edb4e44beee4c55550aad8d3592f4.png)" :question/worked-solution "The two angles marked in the diagram are vertical. Since vertical angles are congruent, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}
3x - 15^{∘} &= 2x + 10^{∘} \\
x - 15^{∘} &= 10^{∘} \\
x &= 25^{∘}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we know $x=25^\circ$, we can substitute into one of the expressions to calculate the measure of the angles. Let's substitute into the expression $2x + 10^\circ$:

$$
2x + 10^\circ = 2 \cdot 25^\circ + 10^\circ = 60^\circ
$$

Therefore, both angles have a measure of $60^\circ$."} {:db/id 17592186111082 :question/id #uuid "be0f6f05-9fed-5092-b2db-1e4684f4541c" :question/math-academy-id "q-26276"} {:db/id 17592186111083 :question/id #uuid "c6977140-15d1-5493-9917-edd7c6216236" :question/math-academy-id "q-26277"} {:db/id 17592186110751 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110384 :question/id #uuid "02660015-d4fd-53f3-b7a5-4a4118e406b3" :question/math-academy-id "e-2583"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f0fce9a0-b7fc-51b1-9335-f8853d0d8fe9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048723} {:db/id 17592186050494}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186111087 :question/id #uuid "759f0b46-4274-5bf2-905e-582f2a5a1170" :question/math-academy-id "q-26306"} {:db/id 17592186111088 :question/id #uuid "f4cd868c-8743-5ec2-979a-bb9598c29be5" :question/math-academy-id "q-26307"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Unknown Angle by Combining Properties of Straight and Vertical Angles"} {:db/id 17592186110384 :question/id #uuid "02660015-d4fd-53f3-b7a5-4a4118e406b3" :question/math-academy-id "e-2583" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186110751 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f0fce9a0-b7fc-51b1-9335-f8853d0d8fe9" :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Unknown Angle by Combining Properties of Straight and Vertical Angles"}] :question/problem "In the figure below, $\angle AOB$ is a straight angle. Determine $m \angle AOD$.

![](images/6e/6eac6c11dcc513cdf896cdfaa9650689af1bf58afd147783d0bb1ca61dd3a324.png)" :question/worked-solution "Since $\angle AOB$ is straight,

$$
m\angle AOB = 180^\circ
$$

So by the angle addition postulate, we have

$$
m\angle AOC + m\angle BOC = 180^\circ
$$

Substituting the given expressions into the above, we can solve for $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(5x + 100^{∘}) + 11x &= 180^{∘} \\
16x + 100^{∘} &= 180^{∘} \\
16x &= 80^{∘} \\
x &= 5^{∘}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we know $x=5^\circ$, we can calculate $m \angle COB$ as follows:

$$
m \angle COB = 11(5^\circ) = 55^\circ
$$

Finally, since the angles $\angle AOD$ and $\angle COB$ are vertical angles, they have the same measure:

$$
m \angle AOD = m \angle COB = 55^\circ
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050494} {:db/id 17592186111087 :question/id #uuid "759f0b46-4274-5bf2-905e-582f2a5a1170" :question/math-academy-id "q-26306"} {:db/id 17592186111088 :question/id #uuid "f4cd868c-8743-5ec2-979a-bb9598c29be5" :question/math-academy-id "q-26307"} {:db/id 17592186110753 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110385 :question/id #uuid "a5dae4ad-b516-5ece-8d12-5805c5073fe9" :question/math-academy-id "e-2587"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "44a00376-bac8-5b09-baff-5dfd613c3222" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186111243 :question/id #uuid "40bf6049-ff54-544c-b191-5bb336ee726f" :question/math-academy-id "q-52696"} {:db/id 17592186111244 :question/id #uuid "c0205835-c655-57ea-abe1-9452f7357731" :question/math-academy-id "q-52698"}] :knowledge-point/title "Using Vertical Angles in a Situation With Three Lines"} {:db/id 17592186110385 :question/id #uuid "a5dae4ad-b516-5ece-8d12-5805c5073fe9" :question/math-academy-id "e-2587" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186110753 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "44a00376-bac8-5b09-baff-5dfd613c3222" :knowledge-point/title "Using Vertical Angles in a Situation With Three Lines"}] :question/problem "In the diagram shown below, it is known that $m \angle 1 = 60^\circ$ and $m \angle 3 = 120^\circ$. Determine the value of $m \angle 2 + m \angle 4$.

![](images/1b/1bc662904a52724fac28dc180f70088592ff4da181930c6607b1bb590b3ec188.png)" :question/worked-solution "We have two pairs of vertical angles, and we know that vertical angles are congruent and therefore have the same measure. So, we have

$$
m∠1 = m∠2,; m∠3 = m∠4
$$

We are told that

$$
m \angle 1 = 60^\circ
$$

and

$$
m \angle 3 = 120^\circ
$$

so we have

$$
60^{∘} = m∠2,; 120^{∘} = m∠4
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
m∠2 + m∠4 &= 60^{∘} + 120^{∘} \\
&= 180^{∘}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186111243 :question/id #uuid "40bf6049-ff54-544c-b191-5bb336ee726f" :question/math-academy-id "q-52696"} {:db/id 17592186111244 :question/id #uuid "c0205835-c655-57ea-abe1-9452f7357731" :question/math-academy-id "q-52698"} {:db/id 17592186048174} {:db/id 17592186048294} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186111726} :activity/id #uuid "823419db-8de6-590e-8d12-60c4a4921be8" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050889 :topic/id #uuid "6ea4a4a8-a41b-576b-b701-36d0b9902524" :topic/math-academy-id 1507} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186111428 :step/content {:db/id 17592186110547 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110436 :question/id #uuid "11f90b96-0b4d-5f8d-8b0d-b4cde31fc7fd" :question/math-academy-id "e-3044"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2f6b7437-6922-58bd-a819-de7fb02a261e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050532}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186111084} {:db/id 17592186111085}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating an Unknown Quantity Using Vertical Angles"} :step/id #uuid "fc9b2937-76b3-5f60-a004-4e4ea833b4db" :step/math-academy-id 10143 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111727}} {:db/id 17592186111726 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111838 :tutorial/content "When two lines meet at a point, they create two pairs of opposite angles. Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$  

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$"} {:db/id 17592186269174 :question/id #uuid "6aad317f-209e-580e-8101-2d395c89970f" :question/math-academy-id "q-138086" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198443 :knowledge-point/id #uuid of our quadratic form:
![](images/fa/fab48c5c9c4d9adee4f270c6138d0f69317cfa59ad9d6f5dab2d4cad15d368c6.png)

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\dfrac{x_1^2}{1^2}+\dfrac{x_2^2}{4^2}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=1$ (along the $x_1$-axis) and $b=4$ (along the $x_2$-axis). 

If we introduce new variables

$\qquad$ $y_1={x_1} \quad$ and $\quad y_2 = \dfrac{x_2}{4},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into $y_1^2+y_2^2 = 1,$ or $\|\mathbf{y}\|=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 
![](images/30/3042cf8eadb699a70b70daced51411fa570ec9cdf3b7b270943fe790739a5364.png) 

we obtain that $\mathbf{x} = P \mathbf{y}.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = (P\mathbf{y})^T A \, (P\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{y}^T \! (P^TAP) \mathbf{y}= Q'(\mathbf{y}).
$$

As a result, since $P^T=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}16 & 8 \\ 8 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 8 \\ 32 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 32 \\ 32 & 16\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimise $Q'(\mathbf{y})$ when $\| \mathbf{y} \|=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}16-\lambda  & 32 \\ 32 & 16-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (16-\lambda )(16-\lambda )-1\,024 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-32\lambda -768 & =0 \\ (\lambda -48)(\lambda +16) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =48,\,-16\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\min \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \: \| \mathbf{y} \|=1 \} = \lambda_{\textrm{min}} = -16.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{min}}=-16{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-16I) & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 32 \\ 32 & 16\end{aligned}]+16[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}32 & 32 \\ 32 & 32\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-16I))\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](images/df/df1ad3d9484608d37e762f74d2a61776c8f82f8eb650dcb0a37f47c5037678c4.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v} \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](images/c8/c869aa1eb73c078eaac66201b1062b2d55a45d90ec2010b6af532ca601498a53.png) 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048300} {:db/id 17592186049456} {:db/id 17592186198684 :question/id #uuid "38171cb4-52a5-5ebe-b692-159c5b30da34" :question/math-academy-id "q-170138" :knowledge-point/_questions
