$Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $9{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $40.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ -6 & 12\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -12 \\ -12 & 36\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $40,$ we have

$$
max{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1}={\lambda }_{max}=40.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=40:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-40I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -12 \\ -12 & 36\end{aligned}]-40[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-36 & -12 \\ -12 & -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-40I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198685 :question/id #uuid "8a89d201-6c7f-5b6a-9c34-e445b93c0f7e" :question/math-academy-id "q-170160"} {:db/id 17592186284641 :question/id #uuid "80991c77-0c00-52ac-bae2-41a3b83ff730" :question/math-academy-id "q-170515" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "01f3ea30-3f9d-5508-ab40-ee2dba4f0888" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "70" :db/id 17592186281708} {:answer/id #uuid "2a5452df-294d-5701-b4af-bbf16d6e0530" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "50" :db/id 17592186282056} {:answer/id #uuid "4e6d984c-3905-5e24-bf07-c5dd11a46a31" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "100" :db/id 17592186282364} {:answer/id #uuid "bb2908d2-0e8d-5999-a64a-a03cd4b68ae9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "90" :db/id 17592186283306} {:answer/id #uuid "c1eb5798-946a-56c8-9937-6c6a91e2207e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "80" :db/id 17592186283374}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186283306} :answer-field/id #uuid "e3ab9ad5-298c-5e24-9d44-dc14f057d818" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284336}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find the maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-18{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+81{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that ${x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=9.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "The minimum value of $Q(x)=8{x}_{1}^{2}-30{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-50{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+25{x}_{2}^{2}=100,$ is $-250.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=5$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{5}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}40 & -75 \\ -30 & -100\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-250,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-250.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-250:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-250I) & =[\begin{aligned}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{aligned}]+250[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}450 & -150 \\ -150 & 50\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-250I))y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186389855 :question/id #uuid "9517d41a-5a17-54a5-b8d2-6ea1cb7908a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-179407"} {:db/id 17592186410195 :question/id #uuid "3f433543-b9f1-5f20-b0ed-749a73af3fa7" :question/math-academy-id "q-170506" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1579c753-1597-556d-8bd8-51a8deed3084" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410166} {:answer/id #uuid "1c96736a-b709-578c-8d05-cc73305aecdc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410168} {:answer/id #uuid "31146e93-a5b1-5fe1-90a1-7f9c284f1056" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410171} {:answer/id #uuid "5dd5c912-e67d-530f-a2c1-baaeaac814c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410177} {:answer/id #uuid "a21806c6-2164-532f-ac84-142d42881117" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410184}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410168} :answer-field/id #uuid "5dc24884-5d5e-5b11-b5e7-3763c0022ada" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410191}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}]-20[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get  

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186410197 :question/id #uuid "dea55e7b-1cc0-500b-8640-ae39dddce75c" :question/math-academy-id "q-170560" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198444 :knowledge-point/id #uuid A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]

$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{aligned}]-25[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

:step/math-academy-id 45752 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199396}} {:db/id 17592186199393 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199515 :tutorial/content "If $A$ is the matrix corresponding to the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ then:  

- The maximum value of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}$ of $A,$ and the maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{min}}$ of $A,$ and the minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{min}}.$

We'll prove this result at the end of the lesson.

Suppose we're given that the maximum value of the quadratic form 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-10\: \! x_1x_2+x_2^2
$$

 

when $\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1$ is $6.$ Let's use this to find a unit vector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}$ where this maximum value is attained. 

So first, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ -5 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Next, we find the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}=6{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ -5 & 1\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5 & -5 \\ -5 & -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ 

Finally, dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v} \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

 

Let's check that this is indeed the vector we were looking for: 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({u}_{\text{max}}) & ={(\frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2}-10(\frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}})(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})+{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{10}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =6\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c50ae6a7-1f29-5274-bd82-d2d8acfef6b7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7954 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "08dd4ae6-a6ab-54da-a4ca-840835781b76" :step/math-academy-id {:db/id 17592186389643} {:db/id 17592186389855} {:db/id 17592186410195} {:db/id 17592186410197}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Where the Extrema of a Quadratic Form Is Attained Over an Ellipse"} :step/id #uuid "d2f76172-74c1-501b-a19c-68e6454733cb" :step/math-academy-id 45757 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199404}} {:db/id 17592186199396 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199516 :tutorial/content "Suppose we're given that the maximum value of the quadratic form 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-2x_1x_2+x_2^2,
$$

 over the ellipse $4x_1^2+x_2^2=4$ equals $5.$ How can we find a vector $\mathbf{x}$ at which this maximum is attained?

We can find this vector by applying a suitable change of variable. This change of variable should transform our problem into one where we need to maximize a related quadratic form $Q'$ on the unit circle. Let's see how this is done.

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
{x_1^2}+ \dfrac{x_2^2}{2^2}=1
$$

which  represents an ellipse with semiaxes $a=1$ (along the $x_1$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the $x_2$-axis). 

If we introduce new variables

$$
y_1={x_1}, \qquad y_2 = \dfrac{x_2}{2},
$$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into $y_1^2+y_2^2 = 1,$ or $\|\mathbf{y}\|=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

 

we obtain that $\mathbf{x} = P \mathbf{y}.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = (P\mathbf{y})^T A \, (P\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{y}^T \! (P^TAP) \mathbf{y}=Q'(\mathbf{y}).
$$

As a result, since $P^T=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in the new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, the goal is to maximize $Q'(\mathbf{y})$ when $\| \mathbf{y} \|=1,$ which we do using our usual methods.  

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $5,$ we have

$$
\max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \: \| \mathbf{y} \|=1 \} = \lambda_{\max} = 5.
$$

Next, we find the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}=5{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-5I)\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v} \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e750f422-509a-598a-858a-c11360c80eea" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7955 :tutorial/title "Constrained Optimization of Quadratic Forms Over Ellipses"} :step/id #uuid "f3b4db0d-8fec-573f-8597-7e9b0d0a4474" :step/math-academy-id 45758 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199395}} {:db/id 17592186199404 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199547 :tutorial/content "To complete the picture, let's prove the main theorem of this lesson:

> *The maximum value of a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x},$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A{:}$* 
> 
> $$
> \max \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}
> $$
> 
> 
> *The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}.$*

**Note:** We'll show only the first part (about the maximum value) since a similar argument can be used to prove the second part (about the minimum value).

Let $A$ be a real $n \times n$ symmetric matrix corresponding to a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x)\mathbin.$ As a result, there must be an *orthonormal* matrix $P$ such that 

- $D=P^{-1}AP=P^TAP,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

- The diagonal entries of $D$ are the eigenvalues of $A$. Without loss of generality, we can assume that the eigenvalues are $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \ldots \geq \lambda_n,$ where $\lambda_{\textrm{max}} = \lambda_1.$

- The columns $\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_n$ of $P$ form an orthonormal set of unit eigenvectors of $A.$ So, $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}} = \mathbf{u}_1.$

Take $\mathbf x=P\mathbf y.$ Since, $P$ is orthonormal, we have

$$
\|\mathbf x\| = \|P \mathbf y \| = \|\mathbf y\|
$$

and

$$
Q(\mathbf x) = \mathbf x^T\!A\mathbf x = (P\mathbf y)^T\!A(P\mathbf y) = \mathbf{y}^T (P^T\!AP) \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}^T D \mathbf{y}
$$

for all $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n.$

Therefore, we can conclude the following:

- $\|\mathbf x\| =1 \Longleftrightarrow \|\mathbf y\| =1$ for all $\mathbf y$ such that $\mathbf x=P\mathbf y$

- Restricted to the unit sphere of $\Bbb R^n,$ the images of the quadratic forms $Q(\mathbf x)$  and $Q'(\mathbf y)= \mathbf y^T D\mathbf y$ coincide: 

$$
\{\mathbf x^TA\mathbf x: \: \: \|\mathbf x\|=1\}= \{\mathbf y^TD\mathbf y: \: \: \|\mathbf y\|=1\}  \subset \mathbb R
$$

Now, for any unit vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={Q}^{'}(y) \\  & ={\lambda }_{1}{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{2}{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{n}{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & \le {\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{y}_{n}^{2}) \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,‖y{‖}^{2} \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have that  that 

$$
M = \max \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{y} \| = 1 \} \le \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.
$$

 

On the other hand, if we take $[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & … & 0\end{aligned}]$ then $Q(P\mathbf{e}_1) = Q'(\mathbf{e}_1) = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$ So, we conclude that $M = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$

Finally, since $\mathbf{u}_1 = P\mathbf{e}_1$ we have that 
$Q(\mathbf u_1) =  \mathbf e_1^T D \mathbf e_1 = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$

$$

$$

[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

$$
Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = (P\mathbf{y})^T A \, (P\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{y}^T \! (P^TAP) \mathbf{y}=Q'(\mathbf{y}).
$$

As a result, since $P^T=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in the new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, the goal is to maximize $Q'(\mathbf{y})$ when $\| \mathbf{y} \|=1,$ which we do using our usual methods.  

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $5,$ we have

$$
\max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \: \| \mathbf{y} \|=1 \} = \lambda_{\max} = 5.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e750f422-509a-598a-858a-c11360c80eea" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7955 :tutorial/title "Constrained Optimization of Quadratic Forms Over Ellipses"} :step/id #uuid "f3b4db0d-8fec-573f-8597-7e9b0d0a4474" :step/math-academy-id 45758 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199395}} {:db/id 17592186199515 :tutorial/content "If $A$ is the matrix corresponding to the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ then:

> *The maximum value of a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x},$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A{:}$* 
> 
> $$
> \max \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}
> $$
> 
> 
> *The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}.$*

**Note:** We'll show only the first part (about the maximum value) since a similar argument can be used to prove the second part (about the minimum value).

Let $A$ be a real $n \times n$ symmetric matrix corresponding to a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x)\mathbin.$ As a result, there must be an *orthonormal* matrix $P$ such that 

- $D=P^{-1}AP=P^TAP,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

- The diagonal entries of $D$ are the eigenvalues of $A$. Without loss of generality, we can assume that the eigenvalues are $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \ldots \geq \lambda_n,$ where $\lambda_{\textrm{max}} = \lambda_1.$

- The columns $\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_n$ of $P$ form an orthonormal set of unit eigenvectors of $A.$ So, $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}} = \mathbf{u}_1.$

Take $\mathbf x=P\mathbf y.$ Since, $P$ is orthonormal, we have

$$
\|\mathbf x\| = \|P \mathbf y \| = \|\mathbf y\|
$$

and

$$
Q(\mathbf x) = \mathbf x^T\!A\mathbf x = (P\mathbf y)^T\!A(P\mathbf y) = \mathbf{y}^T (P^T\!AP) \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}^T D \mathbf{y}
$$

for all $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n.$

Therefore, we can conclude the following:

- $\|\mathbf x\| =1 \Longleftrightarrow \|\mathbf y\| =1$ for all $\mathbf y$ such that $\mathbf x=P\mathbf y$

- Restricted to the unit sphere of $\Bbb R^n,$ the images of the quadratic forms $Q(\mathbf x)$  and $Q'(\mathbf y)= \mathbf y^T D\mathbf y$ coincide: 

$$
\{\mathbf x^TA\mathbf x: \: \: \|\mathbf x\|=1\}= \{\mathbf y^TD\mathbf y: \: \: \|\mathbf y\|=1\}  \subset \mathbb R
$$

Now, for any unit vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={Q}^{'}(y) \\  & ={\lambda }_{1}{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{2}{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{n}{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & \le {\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{y}_{n}^{2}) \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,‖y{‖}^{2} \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have that  that 

$$
M = \max \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{y} \| = 1 \} \le \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.
$$

 

On the other hand, if we take $[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & … & 0\end{aligned}]$ then $Q(P\mathbf{e}_1) = Q'(\mathbf{e}_1) = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$ So, we conclude that $M = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$

Finally, since $\mathbf{u}_1 = P\mathbf{e}_1$ we have that 
$Q(\mathbf u_1) =  \mathbf e_1^T D \mathbf e_1 = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$ 
Therefore, the maximum value is attained at $\mathbf u_{\textrm{max}}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "364005f5-f0fc-5d17-9d6b-288d52abe715" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8176 :tutorial/title "Proof of the Main Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "3a8e9986-4b85-5793-91b8-d47f73b67205" :step/math-academy-id 54038} {:db/id 17592186199516 :tutorial/content "Suppose we're given that the maximum value of the quadratic form

of the quadratic form $Q(x)=7{x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{2}^{2}+5{x}_{3}^{2}-4{x}_{2}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $4.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0d7e6a3a-4e90-51f7-9e6d-1f36e15dea08" :step/next {:db/id 17592186410203}} {:db/id 17592186410200 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410197 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27fa6c83-fea5-559c-b3af-e6a7e1618346" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 9\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410169} {:answer/id #uuid "3bb153c6-9455-5e09-b9d4-e4c936682c6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410172} {:answer/id #uuid "566bcdea-96b1-557a-bdcd-81a53378a8b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410173} {:answer/id #uuid "a93b100e-c392-5adc-a3ed-bee963bcaac6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410185} {:answer/id #uuid "b119d151-632a-5e08-8a6e-94f8c7ba763c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410186}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410169} :answer-field/id #uuid "b5b0d1a4-b3d8-5bd2-80e4-83dea5aa94c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410194}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "dea55e7b-1cc0-500b-8640-ae39dddce75c" :question/math-academy-id "q-170560" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $9{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $25.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{aligned}]-25[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3781c4aa-7e7b-5b51-9af4-d354711b0091"} {:db/id 17592186410201 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410195 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1579c753-1597-556d-8bd8-51a8deed3084" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410166} {:answer/id #uuid "1c96736a-b709-578c-8d05-cc73305aecdc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410168} {:answer/id #uuid "31146e93-a5b1-5fe1-90a1-7f9c284f1056" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410171} {:answer/id #uuid "5dd5c912-e67d-530f-a2c1-baaeaac814c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410177} {:answer/id #uuid "a21806c6-2164-532f-ac84-142d42881117" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410184}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410168} :answer-field/id #uuid "5dc24884-5d5e-5b11-b5e7-3763c0022ada" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410191}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3f433543-b9f1-5f20-b0ed-749a73af3fa7" :question/math-academy-id "q-170506" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{aligned}]-25[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3781c4aa-7e7b-5b51-9af4-d354711b0091"} {:db/id 17592186410201 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410195 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1579c753-1597-556d-8bd8-51a8deed3084" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410166} {:answer/id #uuid "1c96736a-b709-578c-8d05-cc73305aecdc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410168} {:answer/id #uuid "31146e93-a5b1-5fe1-90a1-7f9c284f1056" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410171} {:answer/id #uuid "5dd5c912-e67d-530f-a2c1-baaeaac814c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410177} {:answer/id #uuid "a21806c6-2164-532f-ac84-142d42881117" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410184}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410168} :answer-field/id #uuid "5dc24884-5d5e-5b11-b5e7-3763c0022ada" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410191}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3f433543-b9f1-5f20-b0ed-749a73af3fa7" :question/math-academy-id "q-170506" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-18{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+81{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that ${x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=9.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -9 \\ -9 & 81\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$ 

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -9 \\ -9 & 81\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -27 \\ -9 & 81\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 & -27 \\ -27 & 81\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}9-\lambda  & -27 \\ -27 & 81-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (9-\lambda )(81-\lambda )-729 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-90\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -90) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =0,\,90\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
max{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}=90.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "14546d02-e8ca-5bbd-82f2-37c20dd8c152" :step/next {:db/id 17592186414675}} {:db/id 17592186414675 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410197 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27fa6c83-fea5-559c-b3af-e6a7e1618346" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 9\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410169} {:answer/id #uuid "3bb153c6-9455-5e09-b9d4-e4c936682c6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410172} {:answer/id #uuid "566bcdea-96b1-557a-bdcd-81a53378a8b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410173} {:answer/id #uuid "a93b100e-c392-5adc-a3ed-bee963bcaac6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410185} {:answer/id #uuid "b119d151-632a-5e08-8a6e-94f8c7ba763c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410186}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410169} :answer-field/id #uuid "b5b0d1a4-b3d8-5bd2-80e4-83dea5aa94c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410194}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "dea55e7b-1cc0-500b-8640-ae39dddce75c" :question/math-academy-id "q-170560" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $9{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $25.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{aligned}]-25[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "310e7c10-e8a2-5719-93d8-e4b398b84456"} {:db/id 17592186414676 :step/content {:db/id 17592186389629 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "33fcc9d7-da26-566b-892f-8ca0dccbf100" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389631} {:answer/id #uuid "a86affbe-00af-5daa-9d5d-d6b4c732cb8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389632} {:answer/id #uuid "da2b263a-4cb7-517f-88b9-8ca97ec6707e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389633} {:answer/id #uuid "b5f8b750-04ea-55ad-b825-30a6ece0925e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389634} {:answer/id #uuid "0ceac102-859c-568b-8eb7-f0592356b505" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389635}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186389631} :answer-field/id #uuid "205f15e5-0108-5b4a-888b-1b37b338482c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186389630}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8daa1f82-58aa-5738-bbe7-9b509869abcc" :question/math-academy-id "q-170411" :question/problem "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-1.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 8 \\ 8 & 12\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$ 

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 8 \\ 8 & 12\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 16 \\ 8 & 12\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-12 & 16 \\ 16 & 12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-12-\lambda  & 16 \\ 16 & 12-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-12-\lambda )(12-\lambda )-256 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-400 & =0 \\ (\lambda -20)(\lambda +20) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =20,\,-20\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0b1d2308-18cf-5d1f-9792-a558d12df58b"} {:db/id 17592186422487 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198560 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5991713d-c756-5033-8e5a-4d4d4ed69367" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410175} {:answer/id #uuid "5dd4da5f-a084-569f-9c7d-65ba6f2fa2d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410176} {:answer/id #uuid "7a09264a-e062-5b32-b960-ce1fdd0596f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410180} {:answer/id #uuid "a18e2980-f7b3-5399-bdf5-0e6bab2f2d73" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410183} {:answer/id #uuid "f781d714-082f-5b5c-9033-4f6f86bf4d82" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410188}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410176} :answer-field/id #uuid "9a69a67c-d671-56dc-a201-31f05adf2afb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410193}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "13f589cb-239b-530f-99ce-e58d907d8d98" :question/math-academy-id "q-136828" :question/problem "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{3}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-2.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. $$
A=[\begin{aligned}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=5$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{5}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}40 & -75 \\ -30 & -100\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-250,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-250.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-250:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-250I) & =[\begin{aligned}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{aligned}]+250[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}450 & -150 \\ -150 & 50\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-250I))y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}]-20[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "5f8ca3b8-f2b1-5dda-8678-447d69f170dd" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442119}} {:db/id 17592186442119 :step/content {:db/id 17592186378969 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "fea291ee-6497-5ad3-94fc-370909961651" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186378971} {:answer/id #uuid "d36d82c5-f411-510f-b777-9fca82b43277" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186378972} {:answer/id #uuid "34611fcc-fc75-5837-8815-4b563c9bc527" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186378973} {:answer/id #uuid "a08c13c3-88ad-550d-9cc8-cabd76a06564" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186378974} {:answer/id #uuid "a6d304bd-fbab-5bd6-8c82-afcb34c6646e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186378975}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186378971} :answer-field/id #uuid "59fbad7d-97f9-581f-9baa-b0e8b8e58fe8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186378970}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "6d3c8fe2-1d6d-57e9-bf5c-5e70cb30abf3" :question/math-academy-id "q-170561" :question/problem "The minimum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}-36{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $-72.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186180332 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180781 :tutorial/content "When solving a multivariable equation for a particular variable, we sometimes have to factor some terms in the equation to reach the solution.

For example, let's solve the following equation for the variable $d\mathbin{:}$

$$
2cd - 3d = 5
$$

First, we factor out $d$ in the expression on the left-hand side. This gives

$$
d(2c-3) = 5.
$$

Then, we divide both sides of the equation by $(2c-3)$ to isolate $d\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}d(2c-3) & =5 \\ \frac{d(2c-3)}{2c-3} & =\frac{5}{2c-3} \\ \frac{d\cancel{(2c-3)}}{\cancel{2c-3}} & =\frac{5}{2c-3} \\ d & =\frac{5}{2c-3}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** This result assumes that $2c-3\neq 0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "46409ede-9b62-5196-b665-c5ba29062b0d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8665 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "$(9{u}^{3}-4{v}^{2})(9{u}^{3}+4{v}^{2})=$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the difference of squares formula:

$$
(a+b)(a-b)={a}^{2}-{b}^{2}
$$

Substituting $a=9{u}^{3}$ and $b=4{v}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(9{u}^{3}-4{v}^{2})(9{u}^{3}+4{v}^{2}) & = \\ {(9{u}^{3})}^{2}-{(4{v}^{2})}^{2} & = \\ 81{u}^{6}-16{v}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186483362 :question/id #uuid "3eea8cdc-2e47-57e6-a2cc-366fd1162497" :question/math-academy-id "q-5131"} {:db/id 17592186138423 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186138189 :question/id #uuid "eeb682a3-2246-55f7-b99c-f60c589a0587" :question/math-academy-id "e-14337"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "dc7f5072-ef21-5abb-9889-13ab8814af9a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186138992 :question/id #uuid "576307c7-ea1d-594b-a877-222d4efbe86a" :question/math-academy-id "q-55938"} {:db/id 17592186139152 :question/id #uuid "9ba1b73e-76fe-564b-a95b-5d83b106f98e" :question/math-academy-id "q-61981"} {:db/id 17592186483368 :question/id #uuid "4a8a7bf3-5b8f-5a40-b9f8-b1ddba947324" :question/math-academy-id "q-31176"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Product of Two Binomials Containing General Exponents"} {:db/id 17592186138189 :question/id #uuid "eeb682a3-2246-55f7-b99c-f60c589a0587" :question/math-academy-id "e-14337"} {:db/id 17592186138992 :question/id #uuid "576307c7-ea1d-594b-a877-222d4efbe86a" :question/math-academy-id "q-55938"} {:db/id 17592186139152 :question/id #uuid "9ba1b73e-76fe-564b-a95b-5d83b106f98e" :question/math-academy-id "q-61981"} {:db/id 17592186483368 :question/id #uuid "4a8a7bf3-5b8f-5a40-b9f8-b1ddba947324" :question/math-academy-id "q-31176"} {:db/id 17592186048229} {:db/id 17592186048928} {:db/id 17592186049235} {:db/id 17592186049629} {:activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186139340} :activity/id #uuid "0f1320ae-5783-5e37-b1a5-3098937007e1" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049943 :topic/id #uuid "202bf905-577e-51ee-b1b6-25f29f3d77aa" :topic/math-academy-id 2275} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186139340 :step/content {:db/id 17592186139725 :tutorial/content "The **difference of squares formula** states the product of the sum and the difference of two monomials is equal to the difference of their squares:

$$
(a + b)(a - b) = a^2 - b^2
$$

We can check that this result is correct by expanding the binomial in the usual way, as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
		({\color{blue}a} + {\color{red}b})(a - b) &= \[5pt]
		{\color{blue}a}(a - b) + {\color{red}b}(a - b) &= \[5pt]
		a^2 - ab + ab - b^2 &= \[5pt]
		a^2 - b^2 \,& {\color{green}{\checkmark}}
	}
$$

Notice that the middle two terms $- ab$ and $ab$ cancel each other out, leaving only $a^2 - b^2.$ 

If the order of multiplication is switched, the formula still remains the same:

$$
(a - b)(a + b) = a^2 - b^2
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5aaa853f-8b04-5d91-8c05-f30646908746" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8883 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3d09b7a5-02a2-5bb1-ab6c-97fd9a0d593c" :step/math-academy-id 17592186162744 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163177 :tutorial/content "**The chi-square distribution** with $k$ **degrees of freedom**, denoted $\chi^2(k)$, is the distribution of a random variable that is the sum of the squares of $k$ independent standard normal random variables. 

Thus, if $Z_1, Z_2, \ldots, Z_k$ are mutually independent, where $Z_i\sim N(0,1)$, then

$$
Z_1^2+Z_2^2+\ldots+Z_k^2\sim  \chi^2(k).
$$

It can be shown that $X \sim \chi^2(k)$ has the following probability density function:

![](images/6a/6a46942ee5d42c721fb23905e49a67d28c2916eecc234e86734263c599df49fc.svg)

Note that $\Gamma$ is the gamma function.

The diagram below shows $f(x)$ for various degrees of freedom $k.$

![](images/ce/cecc3fc82e618f5b5f91e61c4dcab6c1d38b970af20f0ae2baf929b0ce9cdbb3.png)

The chi-square distribution is widely used in inferential statistics. In particular, it is used in **goodness of fit** tests, where experimental data is compared against a hypothesized theoretical model. You will learn more about the applications of the chi-square distribution in future lessons." :tutorial/id #uuid "8adfa155-2603-5b6f-9206-c73523985df0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10602 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "2249706e-9b5b-5da2-bc3a-0a2a5588a700" :step/math-academy-id 217601 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162745}} {:db/id 17592186162745 :step/content {:db/id 17592186161923 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161732 :question/id #uuid "531bdbe2-35a5-599f-8009-f65888b6f05d" :question/math-academy-id "e-16428"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f80bc6ce-5b86-5883-a2bb-dbdc1e5503de" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049433} {:db/id 17592186049638}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162236} {:db/id 17592186162237} {:db/id 17592186434097} {:db/id 17592186434098}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Probability for a Chi-Square Random Variable Using the PDF"} :step/id #uuid "352f1f5d-a28b-5167-a9a4-4b4ead2412ae" :step/math-academy-id 217602 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162746}} {:db/id 17592186162746 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163178 :tutorial/content "Let $X\sim\chi^2(3).$ Suppose we wish to know the specific value $x$ such that 

$$
P(X\geq x) = 0.05.
$$

Here, $\alpha = 0.05$ is sometimes called the **significance level**. The required probability is represented by the shaded region below.

![](images/34/34551dd57f17cfb0bdd3bebd2d09c907615f3d936e4b5d69083517d17c1f779f.png)

We often resort to percentage points tables to look up our desired values rather than computing these probabilities by hand (which would be very difficult). 

Some percentage points for the $\chi^2(3)$ distribution are given below. Each cell in the table gives a value $x$ such that $P(X\geq x) = p$ for a particular value of $p.$

| $k \setminus p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $3$ | $\,6.251\,$ | $\,7.815\,$ | $\,9.348\,$ | $\,11.345\,$ | $\,12.838\,$ |

From the table, we have

$$
P(X \geq 7.815) = 0.05.
$$

Therefore, $x = 7.815.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fad9ff3a-2abf-529e-b457-a9b2a3922621" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10603 :tutorial/title "Working With a Percentage Points Table"} :step/id #uuid {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the equation of the parabola. From the diagram, we see that the parabola has a vertex at $(-8,-1)$ and passes through the point $(-6,1).$

The general standard equation of a left- or right-opening parabola with vertex at $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),
$$

and substituting $(h,k)=(-8,-1)$ into the above gives

$$
(y+1)^{2}=4p(x+8).
$$

Now, we need to find $p.$ Since the parabola passes through the point $(-6,1),$ we substitute $x=-6$ and $y=1$ into the equation and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(1+1)^{2} & =4p(-6+8) \\ 4 & =4p(2) \\ p & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the parabola is

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+1)^{2} & =2(x+8).\end{aligned}
$$

When the parabola intersects the $y$-axis, we must have $x=0.$ So, we substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the parabola and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+1)^{2} & =2(0+8) \\ (y+1)^{2} & =16 \\ y+1 & =\pm \sqrt{16} \\ y & =\pm 4-1 \\ y & =-5,3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, from top to bottom, the $y$-intercepts are $3$ and  $-5.$"} {:db/id 17592186441441 :question/id #uuid "baa62b58-d974-5e44-ba9b-341e234529fa" :question/math-academy-id "q-73837"} {:db/id :topic/math-academy-id 1132} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186097571 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097855 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to know what are the $x$-intercepts of the parabola below.

![](images/5d/5d3493115eb11315849d3d7c247b9f63a399c6ab7ba2c226b0b84958a47d3a21.png)

Then, we proceed as follows: 

First, we find the equation of the parabola. From the diagram, we see that the parabola has its vertex at $\displaystyle\left(\frac 32, -1\right)$ and passes through the point $\displaystyle\left(1,-\frac 34\right).$

The general standard equation of an up- or down-opening parabola with vertex $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
(x-h)^2 = 4p(y-k).
$$

Substituting $(h,k) = \left(\dfrac 32, -1\right)$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =4p(y+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find $p.$ Since the parabola passes through the point $\displaystyle\left(1,-\frac 34\right),$ we substitute $x= 1$ and $y=-\dfrac34$ into the equation and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(1-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =4p(-\frac{3}{4}+1) \\ \frac{1}{4} & =4p(\frac{1}{4}) \\ p & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the parabola is

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =(y+1).\end{aligned}
$$

When the parabola intersects the $x$-axis, we must have $y= 0.$ So, we substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the parabola and solve for $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =(0+1) \\ {(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =1 \\ x-\frac{3}{2} & =\pm 1 \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $x$-intercepts are $\dfrac12$ and $\dfrac52.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "04c720cc-0a5d-5a6c-acf5-65c378ef274b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3484 :tutorial/title "Calculating the Intercepts of a 17592186097633 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097868 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the parabola $(x-1)^2 = \dfrac 1 2 (y+3) ,$ shown below.

![](images/bb/bbe360c9580cab435e5b737c80c5381f039d1871250cdae3c16bc686e3d0a53d.png)

  

To calculate the $y$-intercept of the parabola (shown as the point $A$ in the diagram), we set $x=0$ and solve for $y.$ In our case, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(y+3) \\ (0-1)^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(y+3) \\ (-1)^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(y+3) \\ 1 & =\frac{1}{2}(y+3) \\ 2 & =y+3 \\ y & =2-3 \\ y & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the coordinates of the $y$-intercept are $(0,-1).$

On the other hand, to find the $x$-intercepts (shown as the points $B$ and $C$ in the diagram), we set $y=0$ and solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(y+3) \\ (x-1)^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(0+3) \\ (x-1)^{2} & =\frac{3}{2} \\ x-1 & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}} \\ x & =1\pm \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the coordinates of $B$ are $\left(1-\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}},0\right)$ and the coordinates of $C$ are $\left(1+\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}},0\right).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f9511803-ede3-5b03-b34f-87d1bb050901" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3905 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3eccc6e2-615b-5126-b1a2-9f9bb514c40d" :step/math-academy-id 23091 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097573}}] :activity/title "Calculating Intercepts of Parabolas" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186096904} {:db/id 17592186097633 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097868 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the parabola $(x-1)^2 = \dfrac 1 2 (y+3) ,$ shown below.

![](images/bb/bbe360c9580cab435e5b737c80c5381f039d1871250cdae3c16bc686e3d0a53d.png)

$$

So the coordinates of the $y$-intercept are $(0,-1).$

On the other hand, to find the $x$-intercepts (shown as the points $B$ and $C$ in the diagram), we set $y=0$ and solve for $x,$ as follows:

![](images/5d/5d3493115eb11315849d3d7c247b9f63a399c6ab7ba2c226b0b84958a47d3a21.png)

Then, we proceed as follows: 

First, we find the equation of the parabola. From the diagram, we see that the parabola has its vertex at $\displaystyle\left(\frac 32, -1\right)$ and passes through the point $\displaystyle\left(1,-\frac 34\right).$

The general standard equation of an up- or down-opening parabola with vertex $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
(x-h)^2 = 4p(y-k).
$$

Substituting $(h,k) = \left(\dfrac 32, -1\right)$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =4p(y+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find $p.$ Since the parabola passes through the point $\displaystyle\left(1,-\frac 34\right),$ we substitute $x= 1$ and $y=-\dfrac34$ into the equation and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(1-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =4p(-\frac{3}{4}+1) \\ \frac{1}{4} & =4p(\frac{1}{4}) \\ p & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the parabola is

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =(y+1).\end{aligned}
$$

When the parabola intersects the $x$-axis, we must have $y= 0.$ So, we substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the parabola and solve for $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =(0+1) \\ {(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =1 \\ x-\frac{3}{2} & =\pm 1 \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $x$-intercepts are $\dfrac12$ and $\dfrac52.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "04c720cc-0a5d-5a6c-acf5-65c378ef274b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3484 :tutorial/title "Calculating the Intercepts of a Parabola Given a Graph of the Parabola"} :step/id #uuid "47e80884-1762-5551-9161-e2231dbed002" :step/math-academy-id 19720 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097572}} {:db/id 17592186097855 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to know what are the $x$-intercepts of the parabola below.

approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=1$ to estimate the value of $f(2).$" :question/worked-solution "The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(1)+{f}^{′}(1)(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $f(1)=-2,$ and since ${f}^{′}(x)=12{x}^{2}-6,$ then ${f}^{′}(1)=12(1)^{2}-6=6.$ So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
L(x)=-2+6(x-1).
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(2)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=2.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2) & ≈L(2) \\  & =-2+6(2-1) \\  & =-2+6(1) \\  & =-2+6 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186364392 :question/id #uuid "7d2c4ba1-9d35-536b-bfbf-3ccc7aa1bc93" :question/math-academy-id "q-75367"} {:db/id 17592186432886 :question/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)(x-0).\end{aligned}
$$

The function passes through the point $(0,5),$ so we have $f(0)=5.$ Also, we're told that ${f}^{′}(0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},$ so we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =5+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(x-0) \\  & =5+\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(\sqrt{2})$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=\sqrt{2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\sqrt{2}) & ≈L(\sqrt{2}) \\  & =5+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =5+1 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the function is concave down on the interval $(-\pi ,\pi ),$ the linear approximation $L(x)$ is above the graph near $x=0,$ and therefore we have an overestimate."} {:db/id Suppose we know that $f(2)=5$ and $f'(2)=1.$ Based on this information, how can we approximate the value of $f(2.75)?$

![](images/25/25baabc5d4193a480d09370faa104d34edc14b2aa09759f5976d592a387fb398.png)

First, recall that the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at $x=a$ is given by

$$
y-f(a) = f'(a)(x-a).
$$

Solving for $y$ in the above, we get 

$$
y= f(a)+ f'(a)(x-a)
$$

Now, provided that $x$ is close to $a,$ we can assume that $y\approx f(x) ,$ which gives us the approximation

$$
f(x)\approx f(a)+ f'(a)(x-a).
$$

We often represent the tangent line approximation using the notation $L(x),$ as follows:

$$
L(x)= f(a)+ f'(a)(x-a)
$$

In this case, we want the tangent line approximation at $a=2.$ Substituting this value along with the given information, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(2)+{f}^{′}(2)(x-2) \\  & =(5)+(1)(x-2) \\  & =x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's take a look at the graphs. Notice that in the neighborhood of $x=2$, the function and its tangent line approximation are very close. The line $L(x)$ is a good approximation of the function for points close to $x=2.$

![](images/c1/c1de31c316c019e8faf466f64a0e6ff24a29935a7ec354c2acdf18d3069b8d47.png)

As we can see, ${\color{blue}L(2.75)}$ and ${\color{red}f(2.75)}$ are quite close. So, we can approximate $f(2.75)$ using $L(2.75)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2.75) & ≈L(2.75) \\  & =(2.75)+3 \\  & =5.75.\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent line approximation

$$
L(x)= f(a)+ f'(a)(x-a)
$$

is sometimes also called the **linear approximation** of the function $f(x)$ at the point $x=a.$ The process of approximating the function by its tangent is called **linearization.**" :tutorial/id :step/content {:db/id 17592186070022 :tutorial/content "A **function** is a rule that takes a number as **input** and then **outputs** another number.

For instance, let's look at the following function: 

$$
f(x) = 3x+1
$$

In this example,

- $f$ is the **name** of the function,

- the number $x$ is the **input**,

- the number $3x+1$ is the **output**.

If we **substitute** a number into our function in place of $x$, we get another number as output. 

For example, by substituting $x={\color{blue}{2}},$ we get

$$
f({\color{blue}{2}}) = 3\cdot {\color{blue}{2}}+1 = 7.
$$

So, the input $x={\color{blue}{2}}$ results in an output of $7.$

We can substitute any number we like into this function! For example, if we substitute $x={\color{red}{-2}},$ we get

$$
f({\color{red}{-2}}) = 3\cdot ({\color{red}{-2}})+1 = -5.
$$

So, the input $x={\color{red}{-2}}$ results in an output of $-5.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "902a3802-7423-5fa0-9cf1-43856055c65c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8783 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "726a2782-726c-5f7e-b8e5-138b8563ebff" :step/math-academy-id 138156 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069579}} {:db/id 17592186069579 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068701 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068486 :question/id #uuid "38228952-21ef-5caf-9805-76e42ebf0caa" :question/math-academy-id "e-14148"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4e5366dd-a374-5abd-bdf6-77f378f97145" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048594} {:db/id 17592186049299} {:db/id 17592186050127}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069041} {:db/id 17592186069115} {:db/id 17592186069123} {:db/id 17592186233385} {:db/id 17592186233396} {:db/id 17592186233405} {:db/id 17592186233561} {:db/id 17592186233568} {:db/id 17592186233575} {:db/id 17592186482561} {:db/id 17592186482574}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Function"} :step/id #uuid "8af30817-9be7-537a-9bfb-2ce31b525422" :step/math-academy-id 138157 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069580}} {:db/id 17592186069580 :step/content {:db/id 17592186070023 :tutorial/content "Functions with more than one input are called **multivariable functions**. 

For example, the multivariable function 

$$
f(x,y)=x-y
$$

takes in two numbers, $x$ and $y$, and returns their difference. 

For multivariable functions, the order of the inputs matters. For example, if we substitute $x={\color{blue}{3}}$ and $y={\color{red}{2}},$ we get

$$
f({\color{blue}{3}},{\color{red}{2}}) = {\color{blue}{3}}-{\color{red}{2}}=1,
$$

whereas if we substitute $x={\color{red}{2}}$ and $y={\color{blue}{3}},$ we get a different output:

$$
f({\color{red}{2}},{\color{blue}{3}})={\color{red}{2}}-{\color{blue}{3}}=-1
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "0bef6d6f-bda2-56dd-badb-0001ca2e4329" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8784 :tutorial/title "Evaluating Functions of More Than One Variable"} :step/id #uuid "004a3461-1ea4-5e28-807b-fea6c51ae3d4" :step/math-academy-id 138161 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069581}} {:db/id 17592186069581 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068702 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068487 :question/id #uuid "4e06fa0b-f3f0-5e60-9a83-67a393b4cc07" :question/math-academy-id "e-14150"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2b5f42de-fad6-54b6-90e1-205fdbe8a456" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069042} {:db/id 17592186069116} {:db/id 17592186069124} {:db/id 17592186482526} {:db/id 17592186482569}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Multivariable Function"} :step/id #uuid "e7679093-39bc-5822-a013-8ae88e7f542e" :step/math-academy-id 138162}] :activity/title "Introduction to Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186068995} {:db/id 17592186069578 :step/content {:db/id 17592186070022 :tutorial/content "A **function** is a rule that takes a number as **input** and then **outputs** another number.

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** ${y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}+8y=0$ represents an oscillator undergoing light damping.
- **II.** ${y}^{″}+6{y}^{′}+9y=0$ represents an oscillator undergoing heavy damping.
- **III.** ${y}^{″}+3{y}^{′}+2y=0$ represents an oscillator undergoing critical damping." :question/worked-solution "Remember that, given the equation of a damped harmonic oscillator, the type of damping depends on the discriminant of the characteristic equation:

- $D>0$ leads to heavy damping,

- $D=0$ leads to critical damping, and

- $D<0$ leads to light damping.

With that in mind, let's inspect each equation.

- The differential equation ${y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}+8y=0$ represents the equation of damped harmonic motion. 
The auxiliary equation for $\lambda $ is

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +8=0
$$

The discriminant of this quadratic equation is:

$$
\begin{aligned}D={4}^{2}-4(1)(8) & =-16<0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the given equation represents light damping, and so statement I is correct.

- The differential equation ${y}^{″}+6{y}^{′}+9y=0$ represents the equation of damped harmonic motion. 
The auxiliary equation for $\lambda $ is:

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +9=0
$$

The discriminant of this quadratic equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}D={6}^{2}-4(1)(9) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the given equation represents critical damping, and so statement II is false.

- The differential equation ${y}^{″}+3{y}^{′}+2y=0$ represents the equation of damped harmonic motion. 
The auxiliary equation for $\lambda $ is:

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +2=0
$$

The discriminant of this quadratic equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}D={3}^{2}-4(1)(2) & =1>0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the given equation represents heavy damping, and so statement III is false.

In conclusion, the correct answer is "I only"."} {:db/id 17592186335726 :question/id #uuid "7c1c35ed-7049-53ec-934c-7b92d30ad741" :question/math-academy-id "q-64616"} {:db/id 17592186357722 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "A particle of mass $2\,\text{kg}$ is attached to a massless spring. The spring constant associated with the spring is $k=10\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.$  The particle is also subject to a resistive force that's proportional to the particle's velocity, and has a damping coefficient $c=4\,\text{kg/s}.$  The position of the particle is $y(t)$ (measured in meters), and $t>0$ is the time in seconds.  If the particle moves with damped harmonic motion, what is the governing equation?" :question/worked-solution "The equation of damped harmonic motion is

$$
m{y}^{″}=-c{y}^{′}-ky.
$$

Substituting our values for $m,$ $k$ and $c$ gives

$$
2{y}^{″}=-4{y}^{′}-10y.
$$

Rearranging the above equation, we get:

$$
{y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}+5y=0
$$"} {:db/id 17592186148177 :question/id #uuid "5e5d3139-8000-5f12-824c-92daaf2b4fdc" :question/math-academy-id "q-64593"} {:db/id 17592186335718 :question/id #uuid
